read.title: Choosing a technique
text: Every differentiation rule has an integration technique that runs it backward. Substitution undoes the chain rule. If an integrand contains a function and, as a factor, that function's derivative, set u equal to the inner function. In ∫ 2x(x² + 1)⁵ dx, u = x² + 1 makes du = 2x dx, and the integral collapses to ∫ u⁵ du = u⁶/6 + C.

Integration by parts undoes the product rule. Writing the integral as ∫ u dv, the formula trades it for uv − ∫ v du. The goal is a simpler new integral, so pick u to be something that gets simpler when differentiated, and dv something you can integrate. The LIATE order (logarithmic, inverse trig, algebraic, trig, exponential) is a good first guess for u. In ∫ x eˣ dx, choosing u = x leaves ∫ eˣ dx, which is easy.

Partial fractions handle rational functions. After long division if needed, factor the denominator and split the fraction into simpler pieces. A linear factor such as x − 1 contributes A/(x − 1), which integrates to a logarithm; an irreducible quadratic such as x² + 1 contributes (Ax + B)/(x² + 1), which leads to logarithms and arctangents.

q.q: What does a good u-substitution need to see in the integrand?
o: An inner function and its derivative as a factor
